meta.warPremiumMethodology: Scenario war spread premiums are model estimates graduated by scenario severity. Sc A (+2wk): markets price quick resolution — modest premium reflecting temporary risk. Sc B (+1mo): base case stress — premiums consistent with observed GCC CDS moves in the week of 28 Feb–19 Mar 2026 (Bloomberg indicative). Sc C (+2mo): prolonged closure — CDS blow-out especially for weak credits. Bahrain Sc C +350bps reflects near-distressed pricing at 134% debt/GDP with no SWF. Kuwait Sc C +80bps reflects GRF depletion and parliament dissolution. Saudi/UAE/Oman premiums remain contained given SWF buffers and investment-grade status. Source: model estimate. Cross-reference: Bahrain 5yr CDS ~380bps pre-war (Bloomberg, Jan 2026); Kuwait ~45bps; Qatar ~55bps; Saudi ~65bps.
meta.hydrocarbonNote: Terminology: 'Hydrocarbon revenue' used throughout to reflect that Qatar's primary export is LNG (natural gas), not crude oil. Kuwait, Bahrain, Saudi, UAE, Oman are primarily oil exporters. Gas prices (JKM, TTF) are NOT directly linked to oil prices — Qatar's LNG is sold on long-term contracts indexed to JKM (Japan Korea Marker) or TTF (European gas benchmark), typically with 6-9 month lag to oil. During Hormuz closure, Qatar loses export revenue regardless of whether gas or oil prices spike.
meta.gasOilPriceLinkNote: Gas vs oil price: Qatar's LNG is NOT directly linked to Brent crude. Pre-2022: LNG contracts were largely oil-indexed with 6-9 month lag. Post-2022 (European energy crisis): TTF and JKM spot markets now dominate European and Asian pricing respectively. Qatar's long-term contracts are a mix — some oil-indexed, some gas-indexed. During Hormuz closure: Qatar cannot export regardless of gas or oil price moves. The price benefit of the oil spike goes to Saudi/UAE/Oman exporters via bypass. Qatar gets no export revenue AND no gas price windfall during closure. Post-reopening: European TTF spiked to EUR72/MWh on Mar 19 (from EUR55 day prior) following Ras Laffan strikes — Qatar would benefit IF it could export. But with 17% capacity permanently offline, the benefit is reduced. Source: BMI/Fitch Solutions Mar 2026; QatarEnergy CEO statement Mar 2026.

fiscal2025.source: Kuwait MOF FY2026/27 Budget (Cabinet-approved Feb 10, 2026); oil price assumption $57/bbl. This budget covers the active conflict period (Apr 2026–Mar 2027). Non-oil revenue rise driven by new 15% global minimum corporate tax (DMTT). Deficit KWD 9.8bn = $31.9bn — third-largest since 1991.

swf.note: KIA manages two funds: GRF (General Reserve Fund) ~$6.5bn — operating buffer, nearly depleted (95% fall over past decade). FGF (Future Generations Fund) ~$913bn — the large fund. FGF assets are LIQUID (globally diversified portfolio of stocks, bonds, real estate) but legally LOCKED — withdrawal requires a parliamentary law. Parliament is DISSOLVED as of early 2026 — no legislative body exists to pass that law. Under war emergency the Emir could theoretically issue a decree, but this would be constitutionally unprecedented. Effective usable buffer = GRF only = ~$6.5bn (~3 months of deficit cover at Sc B run-rate). Sources: GlobalSWF KIA depletion report; Kuwait Finance Ministry; IMF Article IV Feb 2026; Kuwait constitution on FGF withdrawal mechanism.

vulnerability.bailoutRisk: Medium-elevated — GRF depleted ($6.5bn), FGF $913bn liquid but legally locked (parliament dissolved, no mechanism to pass withdrawal law). Key risk: constitutional/legal constraint, not liquidity. Emergency decree by Emir is theoretically possible but unprecedented.
vulnerability.note: Critical nuance: Kuwait has $920bn in KIA assets but operationally can only access ~$6.5bn GRF. The FGF ($913bn) is a liquid, globally diversified fund — but legally locked. Withdrawals require a parliamentary law, and parliament is dissolved as of early 2026. The Emir could potentially issue an emergency decree but this would be constitutionally unprecedented. Without FGF access, Kuwait faces near-Bahrain levels of short-term financing stress despite its paper wealth of $920bn. 100% Hormuz dependent with zero bypass. GRF covers ~3 months of war deficit at Sc B run-rate. After that: forced borrowing, emergency decree for FGF, or spending cuts. Sc C deficit of –37.6% is gross before financing actions — but the $913bn FGF is the sleeping giant that could resolve everything if legally unlocked. EQUATE petrochemical 1.5-month restart. Sources: KIA; Kuwait Finance Ministry; IMF Article IV Kuwait Feb 2026; Kuwait constitution.

vulnerability.note: Qatar faces TWO simultaneous shocks — not just Hormuz. 1) Hormuz closure: 100% LNG export dependency, full revenue loss during closure. 2) Ras Laffan physical damage: Iranian missile strikes (18-19 Mar) destroyed Trains 4 & 6 (17% of LNG capacity = 12.8 MTPA offline for 3-5 years). $20bn/yr in lost revenue. Force majeure declared on long-term contracts with China, South Korea, Italy, Belgium. Pearl GTL offline minimum 1 year. North Field East expansion (32 MTPA, +40% capacity) now delayed beyond 2026 — removes the key growth driver in Qatar's medium-term outlook. Even after Hormuz reopens, Qatar faces a permanent ~4% of GDP annual revenue loss until Ras Laffan repairs are complete (2029-2031 at earliest). QIA buffer ($510bn, 70% usable) provides coverage but Qatar's fiscal position is materially worse than the pre-war model implied. Sources: QatarEnergy CEO Reuters Mar 19 2026; Wood Mackenzie Mar 19 2026; Al Jazeera Mar 24 2026; Fox Business Mar 2026.
